chart.title: The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA Chart), box "TONES AND WORD ACCENTS" (LEVEL and CONTOUR columns)
chart.revision: IPA Chart revised to 2015/2005, annual re-issue (c) 2026 IPA. Symbols and wording are those of the 2015 revision (the 2005 chart with minor wording/layout changes); the IPA page says the chart is re-issued every year since 2025 with only the copyright year and symbols updated.

chart.how_read: Opened the IPA chart page (revision history, licence) and the IPA_charts_E.html download page and its data scripts (charts_fonts.js) to find file names. Viewed the Tones and word accents sub-chart image in three fonts (IPA_Kiel_T_0600.png, IPA_Doulos_T_0600.png, IPA_DejaVu_T_0600.png) and the full chart IPA_Kiel.pdf as images; extracted the Unicode text layer of the full charts IPA_Doulos.pdf and IPA_DejaVu.pdf with pdftotext; read pages 12-13 of the IPA's 'List of symbols and diacritics' (IPA_Doulos_sl.pdf) for names, IPA numbers and hex values, and the IPA_number_chart.pdf. Contour letters were checked by measuring their glyphs on the 600 ppi images. All carry '(c) 2026 IPA' and 'IPA Chart revised to 2015/2005'. Character names checked against UnicodeData.txt of the Unicode Character Database 18.0.0.

count_explanation: The section prints 5 level tones and 5 contour tones, each in two forms: a diacritic on e and a Chao tone letter (or tone-letter ligature), giving 10 + 10 = 20 entries linked in pairs with equivalent_to. It also prints downstep, upstep, global rise and global fall, one form each: 4 entries. Total 24, the same as the 24 IPA numbers 510-533 that the IPA number chart puts in this box (510-511 arrows, 512-516 level diacritics, 517-518 down/upstep, 519-523 level letters, 524-528 contour diacritics, 529-533 contour letters). Diacritics are entered as the combining mark alone; the carrier e is in chart_example.

symbols.articulatory: extra high tone (IPA list name: EXTRA HIGH LEVEL TONE (ACCENT MARK)): pitch, i.e. the rate of vocal-fold vibration, held at the extra high level for the syllable, written as a diacritic over the syllable nucleus

acoustic_correlates.text: F0 is held approximately flat through the voiced part of the syllable (the vowel/rhyme) at the very top of the speaker's tonal range (level 5 of 5); no deliberate rise or fall within the syllable.

Reference measurement for a high level tone: Mandarin Tone 1 (described as High-Level) in isolation, eight male Beijing speakers, starts near 130 Hz and stays around that level throughout the syllable; mean duration 247 ms. After a tone with a low offset, the first part of a high level tone rises toward its target instead of being flat.

Tone levels are relative, not absolute: 'high' and 'low' are judged against the speaker's own pitch range and against neighbouring syllables, and phrase-level F0 declination can leave a late high tone lower in Hz than an early low tone.

Chao's five-level scale divides the speaker's tonal range into five steps; Chao (1956, as reported) spaced the levels about two semitones apart, a later description (Chao 1968, as reported) gave one semitone between levels 1 and 2 and three between 2 and 3; a linear alternative divides the range between the lowest and highest tone F0 into four equal intervals. Use these as starting points, not norms.

Context: the start of a tone's F0 track is pulled toward the offset F0 of the preceding tone (carry-over assimilation, as large as 55 Hz at the syllable boundary and still up to 35 Hz at vowel onset and 17 Hz at vowel midpoint in Mandarin), while the following tone has a smaller, mostly dissimilatory effect; the tone's own target is approached over the course of the syllable, most closely near its end.

symbols.notes: Chart example printed as e with the mark (e̋, e + U+030B; no precomposed form exists). The chart prints it in the same row as the tone letter ˥ (the full chart prints the word 'or' only in the first row: 'e̋ or ˥'); the Handbook (as quoted in Wikipedia) says the pairing is only a layout convenience: with diacritics a three-level system is é ē è and a four-level system adds the doubled marks e̋ and ȅ, whereas tone letters have five levels, so the row pairing is not an exact equivalence.

symbols.articulatory: rising contour tone written as a diacritic over the nucleus (IPA list name: RISING CONTOUR TONE (ACCENT MARK)); the mark's shape traces pitch low to high (L→H) across the syllable

acoustic_correlates.text: F0 moves upward through the syllable from low to high, the rise filling most of the voiced rhyme; the high endpoint is reached at or near the end of the syllable.

Reference measurement for a rising tone: Mandarin Tone 2 (described as Mid-Rising), eight male speakers in isolation, starts near 110 Hz, dips slightly, and rises from about 20% into the vowel to the end of the syllable; mean duration 273 ms. After a high-offset tone the rise starts later (about 35% into the vowel).

Physiological speed limit on F0 change: a pitch rise of d semitones needs roughly 89.6 + 8.7·d ms (Xu and Sun 2002, as quoted), so a large contour cannot be completed on a very short syllable and is undershot.

symbols.articulatory: downstep: the following tone (typically a high tone) is realised on a lower pitch register than the same tone before it, and that lowered register persists for following tones; written before the affected syllable

features.form: modifier letter placed before the syllable

acoustic_correlates.text: Measurable as a drop in F0 between two tones of the same category: the high tone after the mark has a lower F0 maximum than the preceding high tone, with no low tone audibly realised between them (non-automatic downstep, usually from a floating low tone); later high tones stay at or below the new, lower ceiling (terracing).

Phonetically, non-automatic downstep (floating L) and automatic downstep (after an overt L) are reported not to differ (Akan studies cited); size is measured either as the F0 drop between the two high tones or as the difference from the same high tone in an all-high phrase.

Magnitude reference (automatic downstep in Mandarin): the lowering of high tones after a low tone was greater and more robust than plain declination (about 0.25 semitone between adjacent tones in all-high sentences), lasted for 3-5 following high tones, and stayed within about 2.5 semitones before levelling back to the high-tone reference line.

Tone levels are relative, not absolute: 'high' and 'low' are judged against the speaker's own pitch range and against neighbouring syllables, and phrase-level F0 declination can leave a late high tone lower in Hz than an early low tone.

Alternatives seen in the literature: a superscript plain arrow U+2193 DOWNWARDS ARROW, and the raised exclamation mark U+A71D used for typographic reasons (Wikipedia notes this collides with a click-release reading).

symbols.articulatory: upstep: the following tone is realised on a higher pitch register than the same tone before it; also used for pitch reset at the start of a new prosodic chunk; written before the affected syllable

features.form: modifier letter placed before the syllable

acoustic_correlates.text: Measurable as an upward step in F0 between two tones of the same category: the tone after the mark has a higher F0 than the same tone before it.

As pitch reset: after a stretch of gradually declining F0 (a chunk with global fall), F0 jumps back up at the start of the next chunk; the Handbook's Portuguese illustration uses the mark this way (as reported).

Tone levels are relative, not absolute: 'high' and 'low' are judged against the speaker's own pitch range and against neighbouring syllables, and phrase-level F0 declination can leave a late high tone lower in Hz than an early low tone.

symbols.notes: Printed on the chart as an up arrow before the word 'Upstep'. The IPA symbol list identifies it as U+A71B MODIFIER LETTER RAISED UP ARROW. Alternatives seen: a superscript plain U+2191 UPWARDS ARROW, and the raised inverted exclamation mark U+A71E (Wikipedia).

symbols.articulatory: global rise: intonation, not lexical tone; the whole prosodic unit (when attached to a boundary mark such as ‖) or the marked word/syllable has rising overall pitch

features.form: arrow placed before the word/syllable or with a boundary mark

acoustic_correlates.text: F0 rises over the span it applies to (the pitch trend over the intonation unit is upward rather than declining); in English it typically marks yes-no questions or non-final list items, the rise realised mainly on and after the marked syllable.
Being superimposed on lexical tones in a tone language, it shifts and tilts the tone targets rather than replacing them; the raised end is relative to the speaker's range.

symbols.notes: IPA list: NORTH EAST ARROW, Unicode block Arrows, IPA number 510. U+2197 has an emoji presentation; U+2197 U+FE0E (VARIATION SELECTOR-15) forces text style and is how Wikipedia writes it.

symbols.articulatory: global fall: intonation, not lexical tone; the whole prosodic unit (when attached to a boundary mark) or the marked word/syllable has falling overall pitch

features.form: arrow placed before the word/syllable or with a boundary mark

acoustic_correlates.text: F0 falls over the span it applies to; in English a fall on the last prominent syllable typically marks statements and wh-questions, realised as a down-glide on that syllable if it is final or a step down to the following syllables otherwise.
Chunks with gradually declining pitch are the most common prosodic contours; F0 resets upward at the start of the next chunk.

Phrase-level declination itself is small in tone languages (about 0.25 semitone between adjacent high tones in all-high Mandarin sentences), so a marked global fall should be clearly larger than plain declination.

symbols.notes: IPA list: SOUTH EAST ARROW, Unicode block Arrows, IPA number 511. U+2198 has an emoji presentation; U+2198 U+FE0E forces text style.

problems: Rising-falling tone letter: the IPA's own symbol list gives 02E7 + 02E6 + 02E8 (˧˦˨, levels 3-4-2), and pixel measurement of the Doulos SIL and DejaVu Sans sub-chart images agrees (start 3, peak 4, end near 2), as does Wikipedia's IPA article ('since the 2018 revision'). The IPA Kiel-font image (the Association's recommended chart) draws a ligature whose end meets the stave nearer level 3 (˧˦˧). Recorded ˧˦˨; the Kiel glyph may be a font drawing difference.

Wikipedia's 'IPA number' article lists 533 as ˨˦˨ (2-4-2) and Wikipedia's IPA article says the 1999 Handbook chart had ˦˥˦; both differ from the current IPA list (˧˦˨). The Handbook itself was not opened.

The IPA symbol list's TIPA codes disagree with its own hex values for three contour letters: high rising \tone{45} vs 02E7+02E5 (35), low rising \tone{12} vs 02E9+02E7 (13), rising-falling \tone{454} vs 02E7+02E6+02E8 (342). The hex values, the chart images and Wikipedia agree, so the hex values were used.

Contour tone letters have no code points of their own; they are sequences of U+02E5..U+02E9 that fonts ligate. The Doulos chart PDF's text layer maps them to U+FFFD, so the sequences come from the IPA symbol list and image measurement, not from extractable chart text.

equivalent_to pairs each diacritic with the tone letter printed in the same chart row, as the brief asks. The Handbook (as quoted by Wikipedia, not opened) says this pairing is only a layout simplification: diacritics have at most doubled marks for extra high/low and coarse H/M/L contour points, letters have five levels. A synthesiser should not treat é as exactly ˦ or ě as exactly ˩˥.

Downstep and upstep: the chart images show plain-looking arrows. The IPA symbol list and the Doulos text layer identify them as U+A71C and U+A71B (raised modifier arrows). U+2193/U+2191 and the raised exclamation marks U+A71D/U+A71E are common substitutes in the literature (listed under alt_codepoints) but are not what the chart encodes.
Global rise/fall U+2197/U+2198 have emoji presentation sequences in Unicode 18.0; U+FE0E text style is listed as an alternative, not as the chart's code.

Membership: the section heading is 'Tones and word accents', but no symbol is specific to word accents (pitch accent); all 24 printed symbols are counted. Global rise and fall are intonation marks and downstep and upstep are register shifts, not tones, but the chart prints all four in this section, so they are included here. The word 'or' printed between the first diacritic and letter in the full chart is not an entry.

Hz and ms values come from Mandarin (Xu 1997: eight male Beijing speakers in isolation; Wang et al. 2022: downstep). No fetched source gives absolute F0 values for the IPA's five levels in general; tone levels are relative to the speaker's range. Chao's semitone spacing is taken from Wikipedia's report, not from Chao (1956, 1968) directly. Xu and Sun (2002)'s pitch-rise time formula is quoted from Wang et al. (2022); the original was not opened.

No fetched source gave measurements for extra-high, extra-low, low-rising or rising-falling tones specifically, or for upstep magnitude; those correlates are in words and tagged recalled-unverified or rely on general sources.
